interactions.summary: Jiang checks Aurelia's Dante background, jokes about readers who stay in Inferno because hell is entertaining, and gets the reply that the punishments are fun to read.
Jiang explains the reading format and says hearing the Italian aloud is necessary because the poem is built for speech and sound, not silent paraphrase.
Carol reads the English tercet about the mind longing for the lady and burning more intensely when it returns its eyes to her.
Aurelia reads the same tercet in Italian.
Jiang reacts with amazement, calls Dante the greatest poet in the world, and asks for the lines to be read again more slowly so the class can hear the cadence and shifts in sound.

claims.claim: Jiang says many readers linger in Inferno because hell is more exciting and entertaining than Paradise.
Jiang says Dante's poetry is designed to be read and spoken aloud, so you cannot really understand it unless you hear it voiced.
Jiang says the beauty of Dante becomes newly audible in Italian and treats that audible beauty as evidence of Dante's greatness.
Jiang asks for the tercet to be reread slowly because cadence and fluctuation of sound are integral to understanding the poem.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang insists that Dante is not fully accessible as silent text; the poem is engineered for the ear and the mouth.
signature_moments.source_phrase: you can't really understand the poetry unless you hear it aloud
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This line sets up the whole Italian-reading turn in the lecture and explains why Jiang pauses the seminar for sound itself.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang hears the Italian and immediately treats beauty itself as an argument for Dante's supremacy.
signature_moments.source_phrase: This is why Dante is the greatest poet in the world
signature_moments.why_it_matters: The reaction shows Jiang grounding literary judgment in sonic experience rather than abstract commentary.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: Jiang uses it for the audible rhythm and fluctuation in sound that the class should catch by hearing the poem slowly.
